issue_context.title: Filtering openssl list output by provider
issue_context.body:
When I call 
`openssl list -provider-path `pwd`/providers/ -provider legacy -propquery "provider=legacy" -digest-algorithms -kdf-algorithms -mac-algorithms -cipher-algorithms -key-exchange-algorithms -kem-algorithms -signature-algorithms -asymcipher-algorithms -public-key-algorithms` 
it lists all the algorithms including definitely not legacy, such as Ed448. 

Is it an intended behavior?
comments:
List doesn't fetch the algorithms, so ignoring the propquery is expected.

It's seems more than a little counterintuitive to operate this way.  Adding a fetch/free to each of the collect functions would enforce the use of the propquery.
Well... It tries to fetch the algorithms at least for _some_ purposes, I've added it myself :)
It's the command lists that fetch not the algorithm lists.

> Is it an intended behavior?

It lists everything that is present, including legacy *implementations*.  That was intentional.

Do note that legacy *implementations* is not the same as the legacy *provider*.  For example, the GOST algorithms will be listed as legacy *implementations* when that engine is loaded (which can only happen through OPENSSL_CONF).

It's possible that it would be wise to forego all the built in legacy implementations...

I think the question was more about why the `-propquery "provider=legacy"` option didn't achieve anything.

> I think the question was more about why the `-propquery "provider=legacy"` option didn't achieve anything.

Exactly
Because property queries don't cause provider loading.

Ah, now I see... But, what did you expect? If you only load the legacy provider, that property query makes no difference, since all the implementations from the legacy provider have that property defined.

Legacy *implementations* are agnostic to property queries. Propqueries are only relevant for *provider* implementations.
I expected that provider parameters specify the (extra) set of loaded providers and propquery specifies which algorithms/implementations are listed.
BTW, is there any option to list exactly all the features provided by a particular provider?

> But, what did you expect?

As somebody who didn't know the deep internals of the code, I'd have expected only the legacy provider algorithms to be listed.

I know how this works, I know why it does what it does.  That doesn't mean it's the "right" thing to do 😃
Like I said, we could simply drop our internal legacy implementations. They should really not be necessary any more, like at all.
... or not líst them, at least drop that code, unless they're engine implementations
OK, I wonder, what algorithms/implementations are FIPS compatible and expect I can do it using the `list` command.

I don't have a problem dropping the legacy implementations.  I think they should, at least, be renamed to avoid confusion with the legacy provider -- us developers have confused the two on occasion and users who aren't aware of the distinction will find it harder.  We don't need to rename all the internal stuff, just the user visible parts.  What about _compatibility_ instead of _legacy_ for them?

Then we could add a _-no-compatibility_ or _-compatibility_ option to `list` to print them (which depends upon if they are shown by default or not).  We should still list engine implementation regardless (because they need _-engine_ or configuration file to load).

We should also try fetching the implementation as a filter (perhaps only if _-propquery_ is specified).

> Like I said, we could simply drop our internal legacy implementations. They should really not be necessary any more, like at all.

What about some operations that combine external legacy implementation and internal one? Like a decoding an external engine based key encrypted in PKCS#8 with an algorithm that is internal to OpenSSL? I do not even know if we currently support this though.
So IMO it would be safer to just not list the legacy implementations instead of cutting them out completely.
